_doc: Parameters of the network generator (python -m metro generate <id>). Nothing here names a place: the same numbers run for every metro. A metro can override any of them in data/metros/<id>/generate.json (deep-merged). Unit costs, mode speeds, headways, capacities, walksheds and the logit come from the repo's config.json, the same file the DFW model reads.

centers._doc: Activity centers (metro/centers.py): people + jobs per km2 within kernel_km of each grid_km cell; cells at or above min_density climb to their local peak, peaks within merge_km of a denser one merge, and a cluster with at least min_activity people + jobs is a center. Downtown: jobs within downtown_radius_km >= downtown_jobs and peak job density >= downtown_job_density and no bigger job center within downtown_sep_km (a second downtown is a separate city, like Fort Worth beside Dallas, not an office park on the first one's freeways; the region's top job center always is one). Major: activity >= major_activity. Towns (regional-rail ends at the edge of the region): the same clustering at town_min_density / town_min_activity, at least town_min_sep_km from every center. Without jobs data (population-only, flagged) every people + jobs threshold here and in modes is multiplied by pop_only_factor (people are about 65% of people + jobs in US metros: ~0.53 jobs per resident), and the downtowns are the registry's reference points (meta.json metro.downtowns) when it has them, since a downtown has few residents. The DFW values: 4,000/km2 is about the 85th percentile of DFW block groups; a 20,000-person+job cluster is a small suburban office park or a dense neighbourhood.

links._doc: Road links (metro/candidates.py): a Gabriel graph over centers and towns (a link a-b exists when no other center lies inside the circle on a-b as diameter, shrunk by gabriel_slack), at most max_km.road long, routed with the metro and the BRT profile. Regional rail: a route on standard-gauge track from every downtown or major center to every center or town lines.min_km.commuter / max_circuity to max_km.commuter / 1.1 away. A route is kept if it is at most max_detour x the straight line and starts/ends within end_gap_km of its two places.

lines._doc: Road candidate lines are shortest paths (route km) through the road links between every pair of centers and towns; a path is a candidate if its length is within some mode's [min_km, max_km], it is at most max_circuity x the straight distance between its ends and it turns no more than max_turn_deg at any center it passes. Each rail route is a candidate serving every center and town within links.end_gap_km.rail of the track.

modes._doc: Mode choice from corridor density = people + jobs within 800 m of the routed line per route-km. Road corridors: metro if density >= metro and length >= its min_km; else streetcar if density >= streetcar and length <= its max_km; else BRT if density >= brt (BRT that would run over capacity at its headway is upgraded to metro when the length allows); else not a candidate. Rail corridors: regional (commuter) rail if density within 1.6 km of the line >= commuter_1600m. Calibrated on DFW: today's DART light rail lines run 4,600-10,300 (median 7,800), the hand-planned BRT 1,900-7,700 (median 4,000), proposed metro 3,000-12,000 (median 7,200); 7,000 per route-km is about 4,400 people + jobs per km2 across the 1.6 km wide band, near the 30 per gross acre US light-rail break-even (Guerra & Cervero 2011).

stations._doc: Stop spacing (km) by mode and setting: urban where people + jobs density (800 m) at the point >= config growth.tod.setting_density_per_km2.urban, suburban elsewhere. BRT 1.2 / 1.6 km is the rule tools/gen_expansion.py uses for DFW's new BRT; metro 1.0 / 2.0 and regional rail 4 / 8 sit inside the config.json standards.spacing_km bands. Centers the line passes and existing stations within snap_existing_m of it are always stops (shared ids: transfers); stops closer than min_gap_km merge. Explicit walk transfers are added to other lines' stations within transfer_m.

grade._doc: Grade for costing: metro in tunnel within core_radius_km of a downtown center (as the DFW tools cost proposed metro inside config cores), surface elsewhere; BRT, streetcar and regional rail at surface.

sketch._doc: Sketch demand used to rank candidates (metro/sketch.py): commutes (gravity model, or LODES when given) between the walk catchments (walk_km) of a line's stations, and park & ride catchments (pnr from config.access) at regional-rail stations and line termini, each pair's transit share from the config.json ridership logit (drive vs this line's door-to-door time). Value = daily trips the line adds over what today's lines and the lines already chosen already give each zone pair (single-line trips; transfers are left to the full model). Garages cap park & ride riders at config pnr_spaces x pnr_people_per_space.

routing._doc: Street profile for generated BRT (metro/routing.py brt_path): cost per km by road class (freeways and highways dear: a BRT station beside a freeway has no walk-up catchment and no frontage to develop), times a frontage factor that falls from 1 where nobody lives or works along the street toward frontage_min as people + jobs within walking distance (800 m) approach frontage_ref per km2; a highway's frontage roads (by name) cost frontage_road times more, like the highway beside them. So the bus takes the arterial lined with homes and shops over the parallel highway.

selection._doc: Greedy selection: the candidate with the most new daily trips per $M of (capital + value_opex_years x operating cost) is chosen, again and again, until the budget (capital, 2025 $) is spent or no candidate reaches min_trips_per_musd. A candidate within duplicate_m of chosen or existing lines for more than duplicate_share of its length is a duplicate, unless it extends a chosen line of the same mode (that line is replaced by the longer one and only the extra cost is charged), or unless it runs at least branch_min_km on its own (null: never): a branch off a shared trunk, charged only for what isn't within branch_share_m of chosen lines of its mode (the output tables snap stops within 250 m, so those stretches share station pairs and the network splits their cost). Default budget: config budget.musd_per_year x years.

model._doc: Full-model selection (metro/modelselect.py), off unless enabled (or generate(full_model=True), CLI --full-model). The sketch selection runs with its floor x pool_floor_factor (0: every candidate its other rules allow: no duplicates or islands), up to pool_max_lines lines and pool_budget_factor x the budget, to give a wider pool, then the dfwt demand model prunes it: each line's value is the mean of the daily trips the pool network loses without it and the trips it adds alone to today's network, in judge_year (default: the first of generate's future_years, else the year after existing_year) on the land use of the whole first pool open (fixed through the rounds), per $M of capital + value_opex_years x opex. Rounds drop the worse half of the lines below min_trips_per_musd until none is, then the lowest-valued lines until the pool fits the budget. The model's trips are several times the sketch's (transfers, feeder buses, growth), so the floor is its own: 1.0, about the 10th percentile of DFW Transit's 2 million plan's lines on the same measure (results/two_million/line_values.csv: 0.25 to 57, median 4.6, in 2100).

buildout._doc: Build-out mode (python -m metro generate <id> --buildout, or registry key buildout: true): for a metro whose layout can carry a network as big as DFW Transit's 2 million riders plan, and a budget to match. Merged over the parameters above. Smaller and closer activity centers make the Gabriel graph a web along the arterials (the generator's version of the hand plan's arterial BRT grid); BRT down to the hand plan's thinnest BRT corridors (about 1,900 people + jobs per route-km); a lower stopping rule and more lines. Use it per metro, not by default. Tested at DFW Transit's 75-year rate per resident, on today's land use: in Austin with the 2 million plan's policies it builds $28B instead of $17B and carries 5.2% of commutes instead of 3.9%, and in San Antonio $27B and 4.2% instead of $15B and 3.2%; in DFW it adds $17B of BRT ($86B against $69B) for the same riders, and in El Paso the smaller centers split its few strong corridors and it does worse. Neither mode reaches the DFW hand plan's 315,000 trips on today's land use: the hand plan has pieces a corridor generator doesn't draw (the downtown subway, through-running regional rail).
